title: Injection Log Template for GLP-1 and Testosterone Clinics (October 2026)
summary: An injection log template for clinics that give weekly GLP-1 and testosterone shots: the fields to record, where the log lives, and how to retire paper.
body_markdown:
## What Is an Injection Log and Why Do Weekly Patients Need One?


An injection log is a running record of each dose given in the clinic: when, what, how much, where on the body, from which vial and by whom. Weekly patients need one because the order is written once but the doses are given fifty times, and each dose is a separate event that can be questioned.


A visit note answers "what did the provider decide." The log answers "what actually went into the patient on this date." Those are different questions, and clinics that only have the first one struggle when a patient reports a reaction, disputes a charge or changes pharmacies.


Volume is the reason it deserves its own structure. An owner running a testosterone and semaglutide program told us each weekly patient comes in, gets a shot and leaves, and that he did not want fifty-two chart notes of injections with nothing else in them. That instinct is right, and it is why the log should be lighter than a note.


## What Fields Should an Injection Log Template Include?


A good injection log template has nine core fields and a few optional ones. The core set is what lets you reconstruct any dose later without asking staff to remember.


Field Why it matters Required?


Date and time Proves the interval between doses and flags overdue patients Yes


Medication and concentration Compounded products vary, so "semaglutide" alone is not enough Yes


Dose (units or mL) The number a patient or pharmacy will ask about Yes


Injection site Supports site rotation and reaction follow-up Yes


Lot number and beyond-use date Traces a reaction or recall to a vial Yes


Administered by Names the staff member responsible Yes


Order or protocol reference Shows the dose matched an active order Yes


Reaction or notes Captures redness, nausea or a missed-dose comment Yes


Weight or vitals Useful for GLP-1 programs where weight drives dose decisions Optional


Payment status Replaces the "did they pay" column on the paper sheet Optional


The payment column on paper sheets is not clutter. In the calls we hear, owners keep it because the sheet is also how they know who is paid up. If you move to software, link the entry to the membership or package it draws from instead of typing a checkmark.


## How Do You Track Weekly GLP-1 Injections Differently From Testosterone?


GLP-1 injections are tracked around dose changes, and testosterone injections are tracked around controlled substance rules. Both use the same core log, but each needs one extra layer.


For semaglutide and tirzepatide, add the current titration step and the date the next increase is due, because dose escalation is the decision point. Our guide to[GLP-1 programs and pharmacy integrations](https://decodahealth.com/blog/glp-1-programs-compounding-pharmacy-integration) covers how titration, refills and follow-up fit together, and the[weight loss care pathway post](https://decodahealth.com/blog/care-pathways-weight-loss-provider-alerts) shows how to alert a provider when a patient stalls.


For testosterone, add the running supply: how many milliliters were dispensed, how many have been given, and what remains. Because testosterone is a Schedule III substance, the Drug Enforcement Administration requires practitioners to keep controlled substance records and inventories for[at least two years](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1304.04) under 21 CFR 1304.04. The dispensing rule at[21 CFR 1304.22](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1304.22) lists what a dispensing record has to carry, including the recipient, the substance, the quantity and the date. Ask your attorney whether your arrangement is dispensing, administering or both, since the paperwork differs.


If your hormone patients also have labs and refills to manage, the[HRT refill workflow errors guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/hrt-refill-workflow-errors) and the[EPCS and PDMP guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/epcs-pdmp-compounding-hormone-clinic-emr) cover the prescribing side that sits upstream of the log.


## Does a Walk-In Injection Need a Full Visit Note?


A routine repeat dose generally needs an administration record, not a full encounter note. The log entry shows what was given and who gave it, and a full note is written when something changes: a new dose, a new symptom, a lab review or a provider assessment.


Coding sources draw the same line. An AAPC coding alert on nurse injections explains that the right record[depends on whether the nurse only gave the injection or some evaluation took place](https://www.aapc.com/codes/coding-newsletters/my-internal-medicine-coding-alert/reader-question-nurse-injections-article) . Immunization guidance goes further: a position paper from the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends keeping[encounter documentation separate from the vaccine administration record](https://chfs.ky.gov/agencies/dph/dafm/Documents/IIAAPPositionPaper99211.pdf) , with product, lot number, site and method on the administration sheet. The principle carries over to a cash-pay clinic even though billing rules differ.


Your medical director sets the standard for your clinic. Write down which situations trigger a full note, such as a dose change, a reported side effect, a missed-dose gap over a set number of days, or a lab result that arrived since the last visit. Then train front-line staff to escalate to a provider when any of those appear.


## Where Should the Injection Log Live: Paper, Spreadsheet or the Chart?


The log should live inside the patient chart, because that is the only place it is retained, access-controlled and visible to the provider at the next decision. Paper and spreadsheets are the two common starting points, and each breaks in a predictable way.


- **Paper sheet per patient:** fast at the counter, but hundreds of sheets cannot be searched, backed up or audited, and a lost sheet is a lost record
- **Shared spreadsheet:** searchable, but anyone can overwrite a row, there is no signature, and it does not connect to inventory or billing
- **Log inside the chart:** entries are timestamped and attributed to the staff member, tied to the patient and retrievable with the rest of the record


The honest tradeoff is speed. A paper sheet takes ten seconds. Any software log that takes two minutes of clicking will lose to the paper sheet at 4:45 on a Friday, so test the entry time before you commit.


## Why Keep the Injection Log Separate From the Medication List?


Keep them separate because they answer different questions and grow at different speeds. The medication list shows what a provider prescribed and sent to a pharmacy. The injection log shows every dose given in the room.


If weekly shots go into the medication list, a patient on testosterone accumulates fifty-two lines a year, and the provider who opens that list to prescribe has to scroll past them. Prescribing screens also tend to trigger pharmacy and controlled substance workflows, which an in-clinic dose does not need. A prospect who runs on a general-purpose EMR described exactly this when we talked: everything is a medication, but one is a script sent to a pharmacy and the other is a shot at the counter.


When you evaluate software, ask to see a repeat injection entered end to end. The questions to ask:


1. Can staff log a dose without creating an appointment or a full note?
2. Does the entry show the previous dose and site on screen?
3. Does it deduct from inventory and record the lot number?
4. Is it separate from the prescribing list?


Our[med spa inventory tracking guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-injectable-inventory-tracking) explains how lot numbers and deductions work for injectables, which applies equally to vials of semaglutide or testosterone.


## A Weekly Injection Workflow You Can Copy


A workable weekly workflow has five steps and takes under two minutes per patient once it is practiced. The point is that every step leaves a field filled in, so nothing depends on memory.


1. **Check in:** confirm identity and that the patient has an active order and a current membership or package credit
2. **Review the last entry:** read the previous dose, site and any reaction on the same screen
3. **Screen quickly:** ask about new symptoms and missed doses, and escalate to a provider if any are reported
4. **Administer and record:** enter dose, site, lot number and your name immediately, not at the end of the day
5. **Book or confirm the next shot:** so the weekly interval does not rely on the patient remembering


For patients on recurring plans, tie the shot to the payment. A[membership structure](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-pricing-retention) that draws one credit per injection means the log and the billing record agree without a separate checkmark.


## How Do You Handle Site Rotation, Missed Doses and Reactions in the Log?


Handle them with rules written in advance, then make the log show what the rule needs. Site rotation needs the last two sites visible. Missed doses need a clock. Reactions need a place that a provider will actually see.


- **Site rotation:** record the site every time, and show the previous two entries next to the new one
- **Missed doses:** set a gap, such as ten days since the last GLP-1 shot, after which staff must ask a provider before injecting; your medical director defines the number
- **Reactions:** a reaction field that triggers a task for the provider, not a free-text note nobody reads
- **Dose changes:** require a provider's order reference before the new dose can be entered


Reaction records matter beyond clinical care. The[adverse event reporting guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/adverse-event-reporting-med-spa) explains how to document and escalate problems, and a clean injection log is the first thing that guide asks you to produce.


## What Does a Paper-to-Digital Switch Look Like for an Injection Log?


The switch has three parts: decide the fields, import enough history to be useful, and run both systems for a short overlap. You do not need to type ten months of old doses for every patient on day one.


Start by copying the last three doses per active patient, since those are what staff look at before injecting. Archive the paper sheets as scanned files in the patient record so the older history is still retrievable. Then run digital and paper side by side for one to two weeks and compare, so you catch fields staff skip. If you are moving from another EMR instead, the[guide to what transfers in an EMR migration](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-emr-migration-what-transfers) shows which records move and which have to be rebuilt.


One more thing to plan for: the owners who asked us about this were weighing a general-purpose EMR against newer vendors, and the injection log was the deciding feature. If the log is your reason for switching, write the test into your evaluation and ask every vendor to demonstrate it live.

## Final Thoughts on Building an Injection Log Template


Start with the nine core fields on one printed page and run a week of real injections through it. Whatever the front desk skips is a field that is too hard to fill, and whatever a provider asks for twice belongs on the screen. Fix those before you pick software.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What should a clinic injection log include?


At minimum, record the date and time, patient, medication and concentration, dose in units or milliliters, injection site, lot number, who administered it, and any reaction. Add whether the dose matches the active order and whether the visit was paid for. Those fields let you answer a patient, a pharmacy or an inspector from one screen.


Do weekly walk-in injections need a full chart note every time?


Not always, but each injection still needs a dated administration record that shows what was given, by whom and under which order. Many clinics keep a short administration entry for routine repeat doses and write a full note when the dose changes, a symptom is reported or a provider reviews the patient. Confirm the standard with your medical director and state board.


How long do you have to keep testosterone injection records?


Testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance, and federal rules require controlled substance records and inventories to be kept for at least two years. Your state board, payer contracts or malpractice carrier may require longer. Keep the injection log inside the patient record so it is retained and retrievable with the rest of the chart.


Is a spreadsheet good enough for tracking GLP-1 injections?


A spreadsheet works for a few dozen patients and fails as volume grows, because it cannot lock entries, show who changed a row or tie a dose to inventory. Once you have hundreds of weekly patients, a log inside the chart is safer and faster. The risk is the same as paper: records scattered across files nobody audits.


Should the injection log be separate from the medication list?


Yes, for high-frequency injections. A prescription list shows what was ordered and sent to a pharmacy, while a log shows each dose given in the clinic. Mixing them means a weekly patient accumulates 52 entries a year in the list that providers read when prescribing. Keep both, linked to the same patient.


How do you track injection site rotation?


Record the site on every entry and show the last two or three sites next to the new one before the injection. A simple rule such as alternating left and right, or rotating abdomen, thigh and arm, only works if the previous site is visible at the point of care. Staff should not have to open older notes to find it.
